slides.title: Uninformed Graph Search

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Uninformed search decides which frontier state to expand without a heuristic estimate of closeness to a goal. The frontier contains generated states waiting for examination; a strategy is the rule that removes one waiting state next.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Imagine exploring a dark building with a flashlight: the floor plan and legal doors exist, but the beam reveals only the next choices. The same state space produces different traces when DFS, BFS, or UCS organizes that frontier differently. Suppose OPEN contains B at depth two, C at depth one, and D at depth three. DFS selects D, BFS selects C, and UCS ignores depth unless the path costs make one entry cheapest. The state labels did not change; only the priority rule did.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Uninformed does not mean stupid or random. The algorithm still uses a representation, successor function, goal test, and disciplined frontier policy. Uninformed means no heuristic h(n); it does not remove the successor function, goal test, or frontier discipline. Think of uninformed search as entering a museum after the lights fail. You still have the room map, the door rules, and a test for recognizing the exit; what you lack is an arrow saying warmer or colder. DFS, BFS, and UCS are therefore not guesses. They are disciplined ways to organize the same waiting list. The comedy begins only when someone calls a queue random because it refuses to read minds.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Retrieve the Meeting 3 tuple and ask which component specifies legal moves, then identify what new choice a search strategy must make. Lesson 4 adds frontier policy, duplicate handling, goal timing, and path records to the state-space model.

slides.title: Five strategies, four evaluation questions

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: We will compare depth-first, breadth-first, bounded and iterative deepening, uniform-cost, and backtracking search. DFS chooses depth, BFS chooses a level, bounded search limits depth, UCS chooses accumulated cost, and backtracking exposes path recovery.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Every strategy should face the same interview questions: complete, optimal, time-hungry, and memory-hungry. Algorithms dislike interviews, but students benefit. Completeness asks whether a solution will be found; optimality asks whether it is best; time and space measure different resources. Consider a delivery robot. A shallow equal-cost hallway map supports BFS, a massive deep warehouse under a memory cap may justify DFS, variable travel times require UCS, and an unknown shelf depth makes iterative deepening attractive. One application can demand different strategies after one condition changes.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: A strategy name alone is not an evaluation. Each guarantee depends on conditions such as finite branching, positive costs, or a reachable depth bound. Finite branching, step costs, depth bounds, duplicate policy, and memory turn those guarantees on or off. Treat the four evaluation questions like a job interview for algorithms. Completeness asks whether the candidate eventually finishes the assignment. Optimality asks whether the result is the best acceptable one. Time asks how much work accumulates, and space asks how much must remain on the desk at once. A charming acronym does not get hired; the problem conditions and guarantees do. Even algorithms need references, although theirs are usually asymptotic.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Choose one strategy and predict its strongest advantage and most embarrassing failure before the formal comparison. Match shallow equal-cost goals to BFS, tight memory to DFS, unknown depth to deepening, and variable costs to UCS.

slides.title: The graph is not handed to the algorithm

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: A search algorithm normally generates the graph incrementally from the start state by applying legal operators. A real program starts with A and generates later nodes only by applying legal operators to removed states.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: On the shared tree, DFS and BFS see the same children but remove them in different orders. The difference lives in frontier management. DFS and BFS see the same children but place and remove them in different orders. Starting from A, the program applies the successor function to create B, C, and D. It does not allocate every descendant in the picture. When B is removed, only then are E and F generated. Incremental generation is why frontier management matters operationally.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Do not confuse generated with examined. A goal sitting in OPEN has been discovered, but some algorithms guarantee success only when it is removed. Generated means waiting on OPEN; examined means removed, tested, and processed. Those events are not interchangeable. Incremental generation resembles building a city only as travelers reach each intersection. The planner does not pour concrete for every possible street before leaving home. It creates the start, applies legal operators, and materializes successors when their parent is examined. That saves work, but it also makes order consequential: a state that waits deep in OPEN has not yet donated its children to the graph. The visible tree is a teaching summary, not a preloaded warehouse inventory.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Predict the first ten removals for DFS and BFS and circle where goal S is removed, not merely drawn on the page. Locate S in both removal orders and mark when it is removed under the stated goal-test policy.

focuses.label: Goal removal

focuses.phrase: not merely drawn on the page
focuses.label: Removed, not generated

slides.title: Read the frontier state before comparing two snapshots

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The two source snapshots show different moments, so labels and frontier contents must be read before visual comparison. Before comparing pictures, read the selected state, OPEN, CLOSED, and the event named by each label.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: DFS iteration six follows a deep branch, while the BFS image is specifically the state after expanding C. Context is part of the evidence. The BFS picture is after expanding C, not another iteration-six snapshot. Imagine comparing a photo taken after six DFS removals with a photo taken immediately after BFS expands C. Different OPEN contents are expected because both the algorithm and timestamp differ. Relabeling the pictures with the exact event prevents a false conclusion about which method expanded more nodes.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: A screenshot can look authoritative while answering a different question. This is the algorithmic version of comparing Tuesday's weather with Friday's umbrella. Visual similarity cannot normalize two different algorithmic moments; the event context is part of the evidence. A trace without an event label is like a laboratory photo without a timestamp. It may be perfectly sharp and still support the wrong conclusion. To compare DFS and BFS fairly, freeze both after the same kind of event: state removed, goal tested, children inserted, or expansion count completed. Then compare selected state, ordered OPEN, and CLOSED. Otherwise we are timing one runner at kilometer six and another after tying a shoe, then publishing a very confident sports report.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: State selected node, OPEN, and CLOSED for each image, then say which comparison is valid and which would be misleading. A fair comparison aligns expansion count, selected node, frontier order, explored set, and goal timing.

slides.title: DFS examines descendants before siblings

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Depth-first search removes the deepest available frontier state, examining descendants before returning to siblings. Deepest means greatest depth among waiting states, so descendants outrank older siblings.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: A stack or recursive call chain naturally supports this order. DFS packs light, like a hiker carrying one trail and a few remembered forks. Prepending children produces LIFO stack behavior and a narrow stored frontier. With OPEN equal to B, C, D, DFS removes B. If B generates E and F, prepending produces E, F, C, D. The next removal is E, then E's child if one exists. C waits even though it is shallower and was generated earlier.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Low memory does not imply good answers. DFS can dive forever, loop, or return a long solution while a short one waits nearby waving politely. That memory advantage permits infinite descent, cycles, and a long first solution while a shallow goal waits elsewhere. DFS behaves like a spelunker who chooses one tunnel, keeps a compact rope back to the entrance, and postpones neighboring tunnels. This is why memory can remain modest: the active path and alternatives matter more than a whole breadth layer. The risk is equally physical. A tunnel may be extremely long, cyclic, or bottomless in the model. Courage is not completeness; without loop checks or a bound, the brave spelunker can become a permanent resident of the left branch.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Name a problem with a deep solution and tight memory, then name one condition that would make DFS a dangerous choice. Use DFS when depth is plausible and memory is tight, not when shortest-path guarantees are required.

slides.title: DFS uses OPEN, CLOSED, and a loop check

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The source algorithm removes the leftmost OPEN state, goal-tests it, generates children, and records examined states on CLOSED. OPEN begins with Start and CLOSED begins empty; the loop continues until OPEN is exhausted.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Click to enlarge the pseudocode and follow one iteration: select X, test X, expand X, filter duplicates, and prepend survivors. Execute the enlarged lines in order: remove X, test X, generate children, close X, filter duplicates, and prepend survivors. Let OPEN be B, C, D. Removing B and generating E and F gives E, F, C, D after duplicate filtering. B moves to CLOSED. If E was already waiting on OPEN, it must not be inserted again. Parent records still remember which surviving child came from B.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Without the OPEN and CLOSED duplicate test, a reversible action can create an endless ping-pong match between two states. Checking both OPEN and CLOSED prevents pending duplicates and repeated examination. Read the pseudocode as a state-transition contract. Removing X changes OPEN; goal testing may terminate; generating children invokes the successor function; moving X to CLOSED records examination; duplicate filtering protects the graph invariant; and left insertion creates stack behavior. Each line owns one effect. If an implementation produces the wrong trace, compare these effects one at a time. Debugging six responsibilities at once is like asking which ingredient ruined a soup after adding the pantry with a shovel.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Explain why putting children on the left creates stack behavior and why parent pointers are still needed to return a path. Failure occurs only when OPEN is empty; returning a path additionally requires parent pointers.

slides.title: OPEN records alternatives; CLOSED records examined states

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: OPEN stores generated alternatives not yet examined, while CLOSED records states already removed and processed. The leftmost OPEN entry is always next; that invariant comes from prepending children.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: In the trace, newly generated descendants jump ahead of older siblings. The left edge of OPEN is therefore a live promise about the next removal. When B expands, E and F move ahead of older alternatives C and D. Read the transition from OPEN B, C, D and CLOSED A. After B expands, OPEN becomes E, F, C, D and CLOSED becomes B, A. The front changed because children were prepended; the history changed because B was examined; the path map changes because E and F point to B.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: OPEN and CLOSED do not automatically preserve the winning route. A giant explored list can still shrug when asked, how did we get here? OPEN and CLOSED describe search status, but parent pointers explain how the goal was reached. OPEN and CLOSED answer different temporal questions. OPEN says which generated states are still waiting; CLOSED says which states have already been examined. A parent table answers a third question: how did each surviving state first enter the search? Picture an airport with a departure board, a passport stamp, and a baggage claim tag. Mixing those records loses either pending work, duplicate protection, or the route home. One heroic list cannot safely perform every administrative job.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Verify one row transition and specify the parent information required to reconstruct the solution path. Verify one row transition by accounting for the removal, new children, CLOSED update, and parents.

slides.title: Advance the frontier one state at a time

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The DFS trace makes frontier order observable rather than leaving it as punctuation inside pseudocode. At iteration one, A is closed and B is the leftmost waiting state.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Predict the next selected state, then click Next. Watch new children enter the left side of OPEN while CLOSED grows. After B expands, E and F are prepended before C and D, exposing stack behavior. Before clicking Next, cover the screen and predict all fields. At iteration two the selected state should be B, OPEN should begin with E and F, and CLOSED should begin with B. Revealing the state tests the entire update rule, not merely the next node label.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: If your prediction differs, diagnose the exact rule you used: queue behavior, stack behavior, or accidental alphabetical sorting. Choosing C would reveal queue reasoning; choosing alphabetically would invent a rule the algorithm never stated. The interactive trace is an instrument panel, not a slot machine. Before each click, predict the selected state, the exact ordered OPEN list, the CLOSED update, and any new parent links. Then one mismatch identifies one faulty rule. If only the next node is predicted, a broken duplicate check can hide for several iterations. Good tracing converts surprise into diagnosis. Bad tracing repeatedly clicks Next and hopes understanding will arrive by express shipping.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Advance several iterations and explain why the current deepest branch wins over an older shallow alternative. Narrate the next update with remove, test, expand, and prepend.

slides.title: BFS explores the space level by level

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Breadth-first search removes the shallowest frontier state and examines every depth n state before depth n plus one. Shallowest means minimum depth from the initial state; every depth-n state precedes depth n plus one.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: A queue preserves arrival order. BFS is the friend who checks every room on one floor before charging upstairs. A FIFO queue keeps older frontier states ahead of newly generated children. For the same OPEN B, C, D, BFS removes B and appends E and F, producing C, D, E, F. C stays first because it entered before E and F. That simple queue invariant generates complete level order across the whole tree.

kinetics.phrase: checks every room on one floor
kinetics.label: Level-order search

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Shallowest means cheapest only when step costs are equal. A one-edge private jet can cost more than a three-edge bus route. Finite branching gives completeness, and equal step costs make a shallowest goal minimum cost. BFS is the airport agent who boards passengers by zone: everyone in zone one goes before anyone in zone two, even if a zone-two passenger waves enthusiastically. FIFO order preserves that layer discipline because older shallow states remain ahead of newly generated deeper ones. This yields a shallowest-goal guarantee under finite branching. It does not magically minimize dollars, fuel, or danger; depth counts actions. A cheap six-step route can lose to an expensive five-step route unless costs are equal.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: State the finite-branching and equal-cost conditions behind BFS completeness and optimality. The exponential breadth frontier can still exhaust memory before the guarantee becomes useful.

slides.title: One line changes DFS into BFS

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: BFS shares initialization, goal testing, expansion, duplicate handling, and failure logic with DFS. Initialization, removal, testing, expansion, CLOSED, duplicate filtering, and failure match DFS.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Enlarge the algorithm and locate the decisive line: remaining children go to the right end of OPEN instead of the left. Only the insertion end changes: surviving children join the right of OPEN. Compare two nearly identical lines: DFS places remaining children on the left; BFS places them on the right. With children E and F and older alternatives C and D, left insertion yields E, F, C, D, while right insertion yields C, D, E, F.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Small code changes can produce enormous behavioral changes. One insertion end decides whether the search dives or spreads. That queue invariant—not the word queue by itself—explains level-order removal. The DFS and BFS procedures differ at a deceptively small hinge: which end receives the children. Imagine a cafeteria line. Place new arrivals at the front and the newest family dominates the next decision, producing stack-like depth. Place them at the rear and older customers retain priority, producing queue-like breadth. The rest of the restaurant can be identical. This is a useful software lesson: a one-line data-structure policy can change global behavior more dramatically than a page of decorative comments.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Translate the insertion rule into a queue invariant and identify the oldest frontier state after one expansion. After B expands, C and D remain ahead of E and F because they arrived earlier.

slides.title: Breadth is visible in the OPEN sequence

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The BFS trace keeps all depth-one states ahead of newly generated depth-two states. B, C, and D enter at depth one, so all remain ahead of E and F at depth two.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: After B generates E and F, C and D remain in front because they entered OPEN earlier at a shallower level. C stays next after B expands because of arrival order, not alphabetical order. After A expands, the depth-one states B, C, D wait in that order. Expanding B appends depth-two states E and F. Even if E looks promising, BFS removes C next because C is older and shallower. The trace visualizes that invariant row by row.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Testing a goal on generation versus removal can change timing and, under cost-sensitive search, can change whether a claim of optimality is justified. Testing a goal on generation versus removal changes the stopping event and can change an optimality argument. A BFS OPEN trace should look layered even when node names are distracting. Annotate every state with depth and check that the depths never decrease from left to right. Within one depth, parent expansion and child order break ties. If a depth-two node jumps ahead of an unexamined depth-one node, either children were inserted on the wrong end or the queue was reordered. Alphabetical sorting is especially sneaky: it looks tidy while quietly replacing the algorithm with office filing.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Find the first row where every depth-one node is closed and explain what layer appears next. Find the first row where depth one is closed and identify the depth-two frontier order.

slides.title: Advance the queue one state at a time

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The live BFS trace exposes queue behavior with the same graph used for DFS. After A expands, B is the oldest waiting state and therefore the next removal.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Predict the next removal, click Next, and watch new children join the right side rather than cutting the line. Expanding B appends E and F, producing C, D, E, F rather than letting new children cut the line. Clicking three times should move CLOSED from A to B, A and then C, B, A, while new children accumulate at OPEN's right edge. If a new child appears at the left, the implementation has silently changed from queue behavior to stack behavior.

kinetics.label: No cutting the queue

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: If BFS were a grocery queue, DFS would be the shopper who opens a secret checkout inside every shopping cart. Efficient sometimes; socially alarming always. The next step moves C to CLOSED and appends G and H. Use the live trace to test conservation of information. One state leaves OPEN, that state enters CLOSED, legal novel children enter OPEN on the right, and each child receives a parent. Nothing should teleport between lists. If two children are generated but only one appears, ask whether the other was a duplicate before calling it missing. A trace is a small accounting ledger; unlike creative accounting, every state should have a documented reason for appearing or disappearing.

slides.title: Breadth-first removal order finds a shortest move sequence

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: In the eight-puzzle tree, BFS removal order finds a shallowest goal and parent pointers recover the move sequence. The puzzle numbers show removal order; BFS reaches a shallow goal only after earlier frontier entries.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Enlarge the source tree and trace backward from the numbered goal through parents, then reverse that chain to obtain actions. Follow parent pointers backward from the goal, then reverse the chain to recover forward actions. In an eight-puzzle, moving a blank right and later left can recreate an earlier board. CLOSED detects the examined duplicate; OPEN detects a pending duplicate. Once the numbered goal is removed, following parent links backward yields the exact shortest move sequence under equal move costs.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Different move sequences can reach the same board. Without duplicate detection, the frontier grows copies like a photocopier with trust issues. Reversible moves create duplicate boards, so graph search suppresses copies already on OPEN or CLOSED. The eight-puzzle makes duplicate detection unavoidable because moves are reversible. Slide the blank right and then left, and the board returns wearing no disguise at all. Tree search may treat that return as a new child and reproduce an infinite family reunion. Graph search checks OPEN and CLOSED, retaining the useful first or cheapest record according to policy. Parent pointers then compress the explored mess into one solution path. The search can be large; the submitted directions should not read like its autobiography.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Point to a repeated arrangement and explain where graph search suppresses it without losing a shorter solution. Point to a repeated board and explain why shortest parent information must be retained.

slides.title: BFS spends memory; DFS risks spending depth

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: BFS purchases shallowest-solution guarantees with a potentially enormous frontier; DFS saves space while accepting depth risk. BFS orders by depth; DFS orders by active branch, changing both memory and first-solution behavior.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: For a shallow goal with branching factor ten, BFS may store a small civilization of nodes while DFS stores a narrow expedition. BFS may store a whole breadth layer, while DFS usually stores a path and alternatives. Take branching factor ten and a goal at depth six. BFS may retain hundreds of thousands of frontier nodes near the deepest layer. DFS may store only a path and alternatives, but could chase an unrelated branch far beyond depth six. The resource trade is concrete, not rhetorical.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Neither strategy is universally superior. A table of pros and cons without problem conditions is a menu with no prices. BFS fits shallow equal-cost goals; DFS fits deep goals under tight memory but gives up optimality. Compare BFS and DFS as two packing styles. BFS rents a warehouse so every state in the current layer remains accessible; DFS carries a backpack containing the current path and nearby alternatives. The warehouse makes shallow discovery dependable but can bankrupt memory. The backpack travels lightly but may wander far from the nearest goal. Neither is morally superior. Asking which is better without branching factor, goal depth, memory budget, and cost structure is like comparing a canoe with a forklift using only color.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Change one property such as goal depth, memory, or step cost and explain why your preferred strategy reverses. Change goal depth, branching, memory, or cost and explain why the recommendation changes.

slides.title: Match the strategy to the guarantee that matters

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Algorithm selection begins with the required guarantee and the known problem conditions, not personal loyalty to a favorite acronym. Case one favors BFS because shallowest depth equals minimum cost when every step costs the same.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Reveal the shallow equal-cost case, then compare it with a deep memory-limited case, an unknown-depth case, and a variable-cost case. Case two favors DFS's narrow memory footprint while accepting a possibly nonshortest result. Case three demonstrates why a guessed bound is fragile. A limit of four misses a goal at depth five; a huge limit recreates DFS's descent risk. Iterative deepening systematically tries four, then five, paying repeated upper-level work to avoid both guesses.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Choosing BFS because it feels thorough is not a technical justification. Thorough can be another word for out of memory. Case three favors iterative deepening because goal depth is unknown. Algorithm selection resembles medical triage: begin with the outcome that must be protected. If a shallowest equal-cost solution is required, BFS may justify its memory bill. If memory is strict and any solution is acceptable, DFS may be reasonable. Unknown depth favors iterative deepening; variable positive costs favor UCS. State the accepted risk explicitly. Choosing an algorithm because it was first in the lecture notes is not engineering; it is alphabetical destiny.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: For each case, name the accepted guarantee, the sacrificed guarantee, and the resource most likely to fail first. Case four requires UCS because total path cost, not depth, defines the best solution.

slides.title: A bound prevents infinite descent; deepening removes the guessed bound

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Depth-limited DFS cuts off a path at a specified limit, while iterative deepening repeats DFS with successively larger limits. A cutoff says the chosen bound blocked deeper expansion; it does not prove that no deeper solution exists.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Deepening repeats upper levels, but most nodes in a broad tree live near the bottom, so repeated shallow work can be surprisingly affordable. Iterative deepening runs complete bounded searches with limits zero, one, two, and onward. If the bound is two, a node at depth two is examined but its children are cut off. The result is cutoff, not ordinary failure. Iterative deepening reruns with bound three, allowing those children to enter the frontier without storing every earlier breadth layer simultaneously.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: A cutoff is not proof of failure. It means the chosen limit prevented this run from seeing farther, not that the goal does not exist. Most nodes in a broad tree lie near the deepest level, so repeating small upper levels can be affordable. A depth bound acts like an elevator whose buttons stop at floor five. Reaching floor five and finding no goal does not prove the building ends; it proves this elevator refuses the next floor. Iterative deepening repeatedly installs one more button. That sounds wasteful, yet broad trees concentrate most nodes near the bottom, so replaying the small lobby levels can cost less than storing an entire crowd. The distinction between cutoff and failure prevents the elevator from making architectural claims.

kinetics.phrase: A cutoff is not proof of failure
kinetics.label: A bound hides deeper states

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Distinguish failure, cutoff, and success, then explain why iterative deepening can recover shallowest-goal behavior with DFS-like space. Space is roughly b times d while time remains exponential in solution depth.

slides.title: A depth-five cutoff changes what DFS can see

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The depth-five source tree shows exactly which descendants bounded DFS can examine before retreating. The depth-five boundary hides every descendant below it, including a possible goal at depth six.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: The linked teaching animation contrasts green DFS with red iterative deepening; predict the repeated layers before watching. Green DFS follows a branch; red iterative deepening revisits upper layers before extending the limit. Suppose each state has four children and the shallowest goal is depth five. Most generated states live at depth five, so re-expanding depths zero through four adds relatively little compared with storing the entire breadth frontier. A narrow branching factor changes that calculation.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: A bound protects time and depth but can hide a valid goal at depth six with the confidence of a locked door pretending the hallway ends. Repeated shallow work can cost less than one disastrous descent when branching is broad and the goal is shallow. On the depth-five tree, mark every node with both its depth and its status: expanded, generated but cut off, or never reached. A node at the limit can be goal-tested while its children remain forbidden. This distinction matters in code because a cutoff must propagate differently from failure. If all branches fail within the bound, report failure; if at least one branch is truncated, report cutoff. Otherwise iterative deepening may stop early and confidently announce that floor six has been canceled.

kinetics.phrase: locked door pretending the hallway ends
kinetics.label: The bound hides depth

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Ask when repeated shallow work costs less than one disastrous descent and connect the answer to branching factor and goal depth. Use branching factor and shallowest goal depth to justify that tradeoff.

slides.title: When step costs differ, expand the smallest accumulated cost g(n)

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Uniform-cost search orders OPEN by accumulated path cost g(n), not by depth or generation time. UCS stores g(n), the accumulated path cost, and removes the frontier state with the smallest value.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Reveal the priority-queue sequence: start at A zero, insert priced children, remove the cheapest frontier state, and update cheaper paths. Insert priced children, remove the cheapest entry, and update a state when a cheaper parent path is discovered. From A, imagine edges to B cost two, C cost five, and D cost one. UCS removes D first even if D is visually deeper. If a later route reaches C for cost three, the priority record for C must be decreased from five to three.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: The first generated goal need not be optimal. With positive costs, optimality arrives when the goal is removed as the minimum-cost frontier state. A generated goal can be expensive; positive costs make it optimal when removed as the cheapest frontier entry. UCS is a road-trip planner that watches toll receipts rather than counting intersections. A path with three roads can cost more than a path with six. The priority queue therefore orders states by accumulated g(n), and a cheaper rediscovery may update an existing entry. Positive lower-bounded costs matter because they prevent infinitely many almost-free detours before the goal. The first goal sign seen through the windshield is not enough; optimality arrives when the goal is the cheapest item removed from the queue.

kinetics.phrase: first generated goal need not be optimal
kinetics.label: Optimal when removed

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Connect UCS to BFS by setting every step cost equal and explain why cost layers then become depth layers. If every edge costs one, g(n) equals depth and UCS reproduces BFS layers.

slides.title: Guarantees depend on explicit conditions

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Completeness and optimality are conditional statements, so the conditions belong beside the checkmarks rather than in invisible footnotes. The table contains conditional claims, not unconditional badges.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: BFS needs finite branching; BFS and iterative deepening need equal costs for minimum cost; UCS needs costs bounded above zero. BFS needs finite branching and equal costs for its strongest guarantees; DFS promises neither in infinite depth. A depth limit l of five uses space proportional to b times l, but fails if the only goal is at six. UCS is optimal with positive costs, yet a tiny epsilon can still allow many low-cost expansions. The symbols describe growth patterns, not guaranteed wall-clock comfort.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Big-O symbols are not decorative algebra confetti. They describe how branching factor, depth, maximum depth, or limit drives resource growth. A depth limit can hide a goal; deepening repairs that; UCS requires costs bounded by a positive epsilon. Read the guarantee matrix as a legal contract with the conditions printed at normal font size. Completeness and optimality are not personality traits that an algorithm carries everywhere. They are implications: if branching, depth, and costs satisfy stated assumptions, then the guarantee follows. Complexity symbols identify the variables driving growth, not a stopwatch prediction. Big O is a map of the storm system; it does not promise that Tuesday at three o'clock will merely be breezy.

focuses.phrase: A depth limit can hide a goal
focuses.label: Depth-limited

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Compare one row at a time and name the assumption whose removal would invalidate its strongest guarantee. Read b as branching, d as shallowest goal depth, m as maximum depth, and l as the limit.

slides.title: Backtracking pursues a path and recovers from failure

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Backtracking follows a current path until a goal, dead end, or unacceptable cost forces recovery to a recent alternative. Backtracking keeps a current path until a goal, dead end, or unacceptable cost forces recovery.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Picture navigating a maze with breadcrumbs and a list of unopened doors. Dead ends are information, not personal criticism from the maze. Recovery selects the nearest ancestor with an untried alternative. In a maze, the current path may be A, B, F. If F is a dead end, record F, return logically to B, and try B's next unvisited alternative. If B has none, continue shrinking toward A. The saved alternatives decide where recovery stops.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: DFS already backtracks through OPEN. This list-based variant makes path, alternatives, and dead ends explicit, but that alone does not make it heuristic search. DFS also returns to alternatives, but this version exposes path, alternatives, dead ends, and optional cost rejection. Backtracking turns failure into routing information. The current path is a stack of commitments; alternatives are unopened doors attached to earlier commitments; dead ends record doors not worth reopening. When the current state fails, retract only far enough to reach the most recent viable alternative. This is more precise than restarting at the entrance and more disciplined than choosing a random door. The maze may judge our choices silently, but DE ensures it does not get to repeat the same joke.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Identify the most recent state with an untried alternative and describe what information must survive when the path shrinks. Dead-end memory helps pruning but is not a heuristic estimate of remaining goal distance.

slides.title: SL, NSL, DE, and CS make recovery explicit

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The source algorithm names the state list SL, new-state list NSL, dead ends DE, and current state CS. SL is the current path and CS is its current state.

kinetics.phrase: state list SL, new-state list NSL, dead ends DE, and current state CS
kinetics.label: Four recovery records

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Enlarge the pseudocode and watch one failure: place the failed state in DE, shrink SL, and select the next available alternative from NSL. NSL records available new states; DE records known dead ends. Suppose CS is F, SL is F, B, A, NSL contains F, B, C, D, A, and DE contains E, I, H. If F has no viable child, add F to DE, shrink SL, and choose the next alternative associated with the nearest surviving ancestor.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Failing to exclude states already on SL can create a cycle inside the current path. That is less a search strategy and more a hamster wheel with variables. When CS has no viable child, shrink SL until an ancestor has an available alternative. The four records divide responsibilities. SL represents the active path, CS names its current endpoint, NSL preserves candidate alternatives, and DE remembers recognized dead ends. Test the invariant that CS agrees with the active end of SL after every update. When failure occurs, DE grows while SL contracts; NSL determines the next candidate. If all four lists change arbitrarily, the algorithm is not backtracking—it is a spreadsheet experiencing an emotional event.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Explain each list in one sentence and predict how all four change when the current state has no viable child. Trace one failure by updating DE, shortening SL, selecting from NSL, and assigning CS.

slides.title: The current path can shrink without walking back through the graph

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Ancestor information lets the algorithm recover logically without performing a physical reverse action in the represented world. Ancestor records encode logical recovery without requiring a physical reverse action in the represented world.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: In the trace, failed states enter DE, SL shrinks to a viable ancestor, and NSL supplies the next alternative. A failed state enters DE, SL contracts, and NSL supplies the next alternative. A delivery robot need not physically reverse every meter merely because the planning algorithm backtracks. The planner can retract a hypothetical route in memory, select another branch, and then send only the chosen forward route to the robot for execution.

kinetics.phrase: failed states enter DE, SL shrinks
kinetics.label: Path contracts after failure

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: The data structure models recovery; the robot, theorem prover, or puzzle need not literally undo every real-world step. Search bookkeeping and external-world motion are therefore separate mechanisms. Logical recovery is different from physical reversal. A planner can erase a hypothetical suffix from SL in microseconds without commanding a robot to drive backward through the warehouse. Only the final chosen action sequence must be executed. This separation is common in AI: internal search explores possibilities that the external agent never performs. Confusing planning states with physical motion can multiply execution cost and produce a robot that appears thoughtful mainly because it keeps returning to the same shelf.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Compare two adjacent rows and narrate the update using CS, SL, NSL, and DE in that order. Compare adjacent trace rows in the order CS, SL, NSL, and DE.

slides.title: Scrub through the source trace

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The slider turns the backtracking table into a sequence of visible state-management decisions. At iteration zero, CS and SL begin at A while DE is empty.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Move to iteration three, predict the dead end, then scrub forward and watch SL contract while DE grows. By iteration three, the path has grown and alternatives remain recorded. Scrub from iteration three to five and watch two coupled changes: SL loses the failed suffix while DE gains those failed states. NSL preserves alternatives. The current state CS should always agree with the active end of the recovered path.

action.label: Move the trace slider to iteration 3

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: A slider is not understanding by osmosis. Pause at each change and explain which condition in the algorithm fired. At iteration five, failed states appear in DE while SL shows the surviving path. While scrubbing the trace, treat SL and DE like coupled gauges. A failed suffix should leave the path and enter the dead-end record; the selected alternative should come from the nearest surviving ancestor with options. Pause at iterations three, five, and eight and narrate the exact cause of each change. The slider is useful because it exposes history. Dragging it rapidly back and forth without reading the lists is technically interaction, much as shaking a textbook is technically using gravity.

action.label: Move the trace slider to iteration 5

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Move across several iterations and identify the first recovery that selects an alternative from an ancestor. At iteration eight, identify the failed state, contracted ancestor, selected alternative, and DE update.

slides.title: Similar traversal does not mean identical state management

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Depth-first graph search uses OPEN and CLOSED, while the source backtracking method foregrounds SL, NSL, DE, and CS. Graph DFS centers OPEN and CLOSED; backtracking centers SL, NSL, DE, and CS.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Both are depth-oriented, but recovery is represented differently: a waiting frontier versus an explicitly shrinking current path. DFS recovery selects a waiting OPEN state; backtracking explicitly shrinks the path. Both methods may visit A, B, F and then recover. Graph DFS already has C and D waiting in OPEN. The list-based backtracker instead shrinks SL and consults NSL. Similar traversal order does not imply identical records or recovery code.

kinetics.phrase: waiting frontier versus an explicitly shrinking current path
kinetics.label: Two recovery models

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Calling backtracking informed because it remembers dead ends can overstate the claim. Remembering failure is useful, but worst-case brute force still attends the party. Their pruning signals are duplicate history versus dead ends or unacceptable cost. Graph DFS and explicit backtracking can share a depth-oriented visiting order while maintaining different bookkeeping. DFS leaves alternatives distributed across OPEN and prevents repeats through global history. The backtracking formulation foregrounds one current path, its local alternatives, and dead ends. Similar next states do not imply interchangeable code. Two kitchens can serve the same sandwich while one uses a ticket queue and the other relies on a chef remembering every table—a comparison that becomes exciting during lunch rush.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Compare primary record, recovery mechanism, pruning signal, and shared limitation without pretending the methods are unrelated or identical. Both remain depth-oriented and can still require exponential exploration.

slides.title: Move deliberately from meaning to implementation

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The pipeline moves from a real problem to a state space, graph, data structures plus algorithm, and finally a state, path, or both. Begin with a real problem whose goals, constraints, observations, and legal actions are explicit.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: A delivery problem becomes variables and operators, then nodes and arcs, then queues, stacks, priority queues, hashes, and parent records. The state space is conceptual; the graph turns states into nodes and legal transitions into arcs. For route planning, the real problem specifies destinations and road rules. A state encodes location and relevant conditions. The graph turns legal moves into arcs. A priority queue and hash set implement the frontier and history. Parent pointers turn the goal into directions.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: An efficient algorithm cannot rescue a representation that erased information needed for legal or goal-directed action. Data structures store the graph, frontier, history, costs, and parents; the algorithm updates them. The five-stage pipeline protects meaning as the solution moves toward code. Real goals and constraints determine the state variables; legal actions determine arcs; data structures preserve frontier, history, cost, and parent information; the algorithm updates those records; the output returns the required goal or path. An error upstream survives every elegant optimization downstream. A priority queue cannot repair a state representation that forgot fuel, just as a faster oven cannot restore an ingredient omitted from the recipe.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Locate one representation error, one implementation error, and one evaluation error along the five-stage pipeline. The solution may be a goal, a path, or both, so each stage must preserve needed information.

slides.title: Explain, trace, implement, and critique

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Review should connect definitions to traces and data structures rather than reward isolated vocabulary recitation. The representation tab connects states, state spaces, graphs, operators, and data structures through one modeled problem.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Use the tabs to move from representation questions to solution direction and then algorithms. Each group should draw, trace, and defend one answer. The direction tab distinguishes initial state, goal, path, forward search, and backward search. Answer the queue question operationally: after B expands, which list changes, where do its children enter, and which state leaves next? A correct answer ties the data structure to the visible trace. Saying only queue or stack is a label without a mechanism.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Saying BFS uses a queue earns a start, not a parade. Explain which queue invariant produces level order and under which conditions that matters. The algorithms tab requires DFS, BFS, and backtracking mechanisms, invariants, benefits, and limitations. The review tabs ask for layered competence. Explanation states what a concept means; tracing predicts concrete state changes; implementation maps those changes to data structures; critique identifies assumptions and failure modes. Practice one weak layer directly. If queue behavior is unclear, write OPEN after each expansion. If guarantees are unclear, add the missing conditions. Re-reading the acronym ten times may create familiarity, but familiarity is the academic cousin of recognizing someone at a party and still not knowing their name.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Choose the weakest review category and answer one conceptual question plus one implementation question without consulting the slide. Answer one weak item conceptually and then with a trace or implementation detail.

slides.title: A correct search answer includes the representation and the process

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: A complete explanation names the state model, graph, operators, frontier rule, explored-state handling, goal timing, and returned solution. Outcomes one through three cover representation from state space to computational model.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: Trace and implementation skills must travel together: DFS, BFS, and backtracking are not understood if only their slogans survive. Outcomes four through six require implementing and tracing DFS, BFS, and backtracking. A student who can define BFS but cannot predict OPEN after one expansion has not yet met the trace outcome. A student who can trace but cannot store parents has not yet met the implementation outcome. The grid separates those competencies so practice can target the gap.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: Brute force is not an insult. It is a warning that systematic exploration may still grow explosively without stronger problem knowledge. DFS and BFS are brute force because neither uses an h(n) estimate of remaining goal distance. Use the outcomes as preflight checks. Can you model the problem, define operators, choose data structures, trace DFS and BFS, implement parent recovery, and diagnose backtracking failure? A yes should be supported by an example or trace, not optimistic weather. The outcomes connect representation to process because search errors often masquerade: a bad state model looks like an algorithm bug, and a missing parent table looks like a successful search that forgot why it came.

focuses.phrase: DFS and BFS are brute force
focuses.label: Brute force

kinetics.phrase: Brute force is not an insult
kinetics.label: Systematic, not heuristic

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Mark each outcome can explain, can trace, or can implement, then select one weak item for deliberate practice. Dead-end information helps backtracking, but worst-case growth can remain exponential.

slides.title: Choose an algorithm only after stating the problem conditions

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The exit task requires one expansion trace, a conditional comparison of DFS, BFS, and UCS, and a repaired failure mode. The trace must show selection, children, ordered OPEN, CLOSED, goal timing, and parent information.

segments.label: Concrete example
segments.text: A defensible answer states branching, costs, expected depth, memory limits, duplicate policy, and when the goal test occurs. The comparison must pair each selection rule with a conditional guarantee. If search loops between two states, add duplicate detection. If DFS descends forever, add a bound or deepening. If BFS exhausts memory, reconsider representation or strategy. If a shallow path is expensive, use cost ordering. Each repair addresses a different diagnosed cause.

segments.label: Boundary and misconception
segments.text: The algorithm name is the conclusion, not the opening guess. Otherwise strategy selection becomes horoscope reading for data structures. Diagnose one cycle, depth, memory, hidden-goal, or cost failure and choose the matching repair. The exit task is a mechanic's diagnosis, not an algorithm popularity poll. A loop suggests duplicate handling; unbounded descent suggests a limit or deepening; memory explosion suggests breadth pressure; a cheap deeper path suggests cost ordering. Name the failure, identify the violated condition, and choose the smallest repair that addresses it. Installing UCS because the search engine made a strange noise is like replacing a car's transmission because the cup holder squeaks—expensive, impressive, and unrelated.

segments.label: Question and takeaway
segments.text: Complete the exit ticket and preview Meeting 5: heuristics add problem-specific estimates to decide which frontier state looks promising. Problem conditions come before the algorithm name; heuristics in Lesson 5 add estimates, not permission to skip modeling.
